title: Multivariable & Vector Calculus
description: Vectors, lines and planes, partial derivatives, gradients, tangent planes, extrema, Lagrange multipliers, double and triple integrals, polar/spherical coordinates, Jacobians, line and surface integrals, Green, Stokes, divergence.

cards.title: What is $\langle a_1, a_2, a_3 \rangle \cdot \langle b_1, b_2, b_3 \rangle$ in components?
cards.body:
$a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3$

Multiply matching components and add. The result is a **scalar**, not a vector.

Example: $\langle 1, 2, 3 \rangle \cdot \langle 4, -1, 2 \rangle = 4 - 2 + 6 = 8$.
Key idea: it equals $|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, so it measures how much two vectors point the same way.
cards.searchQuery: dot product formula components scalar

cards.title: $\vec{a} = \langle 1, 2, 2 \rangle$ and $\vec{b} = \langle 2, 3, 6 \rangle$. Find $\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between them.
cards.body:
$\frac{20}{21}$

Use $\cos\theta = \frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|}$. Here $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 2 + 6 + 12 = 20$, $|\vec{a}| = 3$ and $|\vec{b}| = 7$.

Tip: compute the lengths first; both are perfect squares here, so $\sqrt{9}$ and $\sqrt{49}$ clean up.
Watch out: this gives $\cos\theta$, not $\theta$; take $\cos^{-1}$ for the angle.
cards.searchQuery: angle between two vectors dot product cosine formula

cards.title: For which value of $t$ are $\langle t, 2, -1 \rangle$ and $\langle 3, t, 4 \rangle$ orthogonal?
cards.body:
$t = \frac{4}{5}$

Vectors are **orthogonal** exactly when their dot product is $0$. Here $3t + 2t - 4 = 5t - 4 = 0$.

Why: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$ is $0$ when $\cos\theta = 0$, that is $\theta = 90^\circ$ (for nonzero vectors).
cards.searchQuery: orthogonal vectors dot product zero find t

cards.title: What are the scalar projection and vector projection of $\vec{b}$ onto $\vec{a}$?
cards.body:
Scalar: $\operatorname{comp}_{\vec{a}}\vec{b} = \frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}|}$. Vector: $\operatorname{proj}_{\vec{a}}\vec{b} = \frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}|^2}\,\vec{a}$.

The vector projection is the **shadow of $\vec{b}$ along $\vec{a}$**: it points along $\vec{a}$ and has length $|\operatorname{comp}|$.

Watch out: the scalar projection can be negative (when the angle exceeds $90^\circ$), while a length cannot.
cards.searchQuery: scalar projection vector projection formula onto vector

cards.title: Find the scalar projection of $\vec{b} = \langle 4, 5, 1 \rangle$ onto $\vec{a} = \langle 2, 1, 2 \rangle$.
cards.body:
$5$

Use $\frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}|}$. The dot product is $8 + 5 + 2 = 15$ and $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$.

Example: the vector projection is $\frac{15}{9}\langle 2, 1, 2 \rangle = \frac{5}{3}\langle 2, 1, 2 \rangle$, whose length is $\frac{5}{3} \cdot 3 = 5$.
Tip: divide by $|\vec{a}|$ once for a scalar, twice (as $|\vec{a}|^2$) for the vector.
cards.searchQuery: scalar projection of b onto a example calculation

cards.title: Find the unit vector in the direction of $\langle 2, -3, 6 \rangle$.
cards.body:
$\left\langle \frac{2}{7}, -\frac{3}{7}, \frac{6}{7} \right\rangle$

Divide the vector by its length: $|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7$.

Tip: check your answer by confirming the squares sum to $1$: $\frac{4 + 9 + 36}{49} = 1$.
cards.searchQuery: unit vector in direction of vector normalize example

cards.title: Compute $\langle 1, 2, 3 \rangle \times \langle 4, 5, 6 \rangle$.
cards.body:
$\langle -3, 6, -3 \rangle$

Components: $(2 \cdot 6 - 3 \cdot 5,\ 3 \cdot 4 - 1 \cdot 6,\ 1 \cdot 5 - 2 \cdot 4) = (-3, 6, -3)$.

Tip: confirm orthogonality by dotting with each original vector: $-3 + 12 - 9 = 0$ and $-12 + 30 - 18 = 0$.
Watch out: the middle component is $a_3 b_1 - a_1 b_3$, which is the negative of the determinant minor.
cards.searchQuery: cross product of two vectors compute example 1 2 3 and 4 5 6

cards.title: How do you compute $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ as a $3 \times 3$ determinant?
cards.body:
$\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \vec{i} & \vec{j} & \vec{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}$, expanded along the top row.

The $\vec{j}$ term carries a **minus sign**: $(a_2 b_3 - a_3 b_2)\vec{i} - (a_1 b_3 - a_3 b_1)\vec{j} + (a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)\vec{k}$.

Mnemonic: cover a column, cross-multiply the rest, and flip the sign on the middle one.
cards.searchQuery: cross product determinant i j k expansion

cards.title: Find the area of the triangle with vertices $A(1,0,0)$, $B(0,2,0)$ and $C(0,0,3)$.
cards.body:
$\frac{7}{2}$

The area is $\frac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}|$. Here $\overrightarrow{AB} = \langle -1, 2, 0 \rangle$, $\overrightarrow{AC} = \langle -1, 0, 3 \rangle$, and the cross product is $\langle 6, 3, 2 \rangle$ with length $\sqrt{36 + 9 + 4} = 7$.

Watch out: do not forget the factor $\frac{1}{2}$; the cross product's length is the parallelogram's area.
cards.searchQuery: area of triangle from three points cross product 3D

cards.title: What does $|\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})|$ measure, and what does it tell you when it is $0$?
cards.body:
The **volume of the parallelepiped** spanned by $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$.

It equals the absolute value of the $3 \times 3$ determinant whose rows are the three vectors. If it is $0$, the vectors are **coplanar**.

Why: $|\vec{b} \times \vec{c}|$ is the base area and $|\vec{a}\cdot\hat{n}|$ is the height along the base's normal.
cards.searchQuery: scalar triple product volume parallelepiped coplanar vectors

cards.title: Find the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle$, $\langle 1, 2, 0 \rangle$ and $\langle 1, 1, 3 \rangle$.
cards.body:
$6$

The determinant of the matrix with these rows is triangular, so it is the product of the diagonal entries: $1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 = 6$.

Tip: take the absolute value, since a determinant can be negative but volume cannot.
cards.searchQuery: volume of parallelepiped determinant three vectors example

cards.title: What is the vector equation of the line through the point with position vector $\vec{r}_0$ in direction $\vec{v}$?
cards.body:
$\vec{r}(t) = \vec{r}_0 + t\vec{v}$, for $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

In components, with $\vec{r}_0 = \langle x_0, y_0, z_0 \rangle$ and $\vec{v} = \langle a, b, c \rangle$: $x = x_0 + at$, $y = y_0 + bt$, $z = z_0 + ct$.

Watch out: the parametrization of a line is not unique; any point on it and any nonzero multiple of $\vec{v}$ also works.
cards.searchQuery: vector equation of a line parametric equations 3D

cards.title: Give a direction vector for the line through $(1, 2, 3)$ and $(4, 0, 5)$.
cards.body:
$\langle 3, -2, 2 \rangle$

Subtract the points: $\langle 4 - 1,\ 0 - 2,\ 5 - 3 \rangle$.

Example: one parametrization is $\vec{r}(t) = \langle 1 + 3t,\ 2 - 2t,\ 3 + 2t \rangle$, which hits the second point at $t = 1$.
Watch out: any nonzero multiple, such as $\langle -3, 2, -2 \rangle$, is also a valid direction.
cards.searchQuery: direction vector of line through two points 3D

cards.title: What are the symmetric equations of the line through $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ with direction $\langle a, b, c \rangle$?
cards.body:
$\frac{x - x_0}{a} = \frac{y - y_0}{b} = \frac{z - z_0}{c}$

Solve each parametric equation for $t$ and set them equal. This needs $a$, $b$ and $c$ all nonzero.

Watch out: if, say, $c = 0$, write $z = z_0$ separately and keep the other two ratios equal.
cards.searchQuery: symmetric equations of a line in space

cards.title: What is the equation of the plane through $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ with normal vector $\langle a, b, c \rangle$?
cards.body:
$a(x - x_0) + b(y - y_0) + c(z - z_0) = 0$

This says $\vec{n} \cdot (\vec{r} - \vec{r}_0) = 0$: every vector lying in the plane is perpendicular to the normal.

Tip: expand to get the scalar form $ax + by + cz = d$; the coefficients are the normal vector.
cards.searchQuery: equation of a plane point normal vector form

cards.title: Give a normal vector to the plane $2x - 3y + z = 7$.
cards.body:
$\langle 2, -3, 1 \rangle$

In $ax + by + cz = d$ the coefficients $\langle a, b, c \rangle$ form a normal vector.

Watch out: the constant $7$ does not affect the normal; it only shifts the plane. Any nonzero multiple of the normal also works.
cards.searchQuery: normal vector to plane from equation coefficients

cards.title: Find the plane through $(1, 0, 0)$, $(0, 1, 0)$ and $(0, 0, 1)$.
cards.body:
$x + y + z = 1$

Two in-plane vectors are $\langle -1, 1, 0 \rangle$ and $\langle -1, 0, 1 \rangle$; their cross product is $\langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle$, the normal. Using the point $(1, 0, 0)$ gives $x + y + z = 1$.

Tip: general recipe: take the cross product of two in-plane vectors to get $\vec{n}$, then use point-normal form.
cards.searchQuery: plane through three points cross product normal vector

cards.title: What is the distance from $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ to the plane $ax + by + cz + d = 0$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{|a x_1 + b y_1 + c z_1 + d|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}$

This is the length of the projection of a vector from any point on the plane to $P_1$ onto the unit normal.

Example: the distance from $(1, 2, 3)$ to $x + 2y + 2z = 0$ is $\frac{|1 + 4 + 6|}{3} = \frac{11}{3}$.
Watch out: write the plane with everything on one side first, so $d$ carries the right sign.
cards.searchQuery: distance from point to plane formula

cards.title: Where does the line $\vec{r}(t) = \langle 1 + t,\ 2t,\ 3 - t \rangle$ meet the plane $x + y + z = 6$? Give the point.
cards.body:
$(2, 2, 2)$

Substitute into the plane: $(1 + t) + 2t + (3 - t) = 4 + 2t = 6$, so $t = 1$. Then $\vec{r}(1) = \langle 2, 2, 2 \rangle$.

Tip: always substitute the parametric equations into the plane, solve for $t$, then plug $t$ back in.
cards.searchQuery: intersection of line and plane parametric substitute

cards.title: How do you find a direction vector for the line where two non-parallel planes meet?
cards.body:
Take $\vec{n}_1 \times \vec{n}_2$, the cross product of the two normals.

The line lies in both planes, so it is perpendicular to both normals. Then find any one point on both planes (for instance by setting one variable to $0$) to finish the line.

Watch out: if $\vec{n}_1 \times \vec{n}_2 = \vec{0}$, the planes are parallel and there is no line.
cards.searchQuery: line of intersection of two planes direction cross product normals

cards.title: $\theta$ is the angle between vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$. What is $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$?
cards.body:
$|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta$

This is the **area of the parallelogram** spanned by $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$. The vector $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ is orthogonal to both (right-hand rule), and $\vec{b} \times \vec{a} = -(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$.

Why: $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \vec{0}$ exactly when $\vec{a} \parallel \vec{b}$, since then $\sin\theta = 0$.
Watch out: compare $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, a scalar that is $0$ when $\vec{a} \perp \vec{b}$.
cards.searchQuery: cross product magnitude parallelogram area sin theta

cards.title: For $f(x, y) = x^2 y^3$, find $f_{xy}$.
cards.body:
$6xy^2$

First $f_x = 2xy^3$, then differentiate that in $y$: $f_{xy} = 6xy^2$.

Key idea: **Clairaut's Theorem** says $f_{xy} = f_{yx}$ whenever the mixed partials are continuous. Check: $f_y = 3x^2y^2$, and $(f_y)_x = 6xy^2$.
Tip: when the two orders differ in difficulty, pick the easier one.
cards.searchQuery: mixed partial derivatives Clairaut theorem example

cards.title: Find the tangent plane to $z = x^2 + y^2$ at $(1, 2, 5)$ in the form $z = \dots$
cards.body:
$z = 2x + 4y - 5$

Formula: $z - z_0 = f_x(a, b)(x - a) + f_y(a, b)(y - b)$. Here $f_x = 2x = 2$ and $f_y = 2y = 4$ at $(1, 2)$, so $z - 5 = 2(x - 1) + 4(y - 2)$.

Example: expanding gives $z = 2x + 4y - 2 - 8 + 5 = 2x + 4y - 5$.
Tip: plug the point back in to check: $2 + 8 - 5 = 5$.
cards.searchQuery: tangent plane to surface z = f(x,y) formula example

cards.title: Let $f(x, y) = x^2 y$. Find the directional derivative at $(1, 3)$ in the direction of $\vec{v} = \langle 3, 4 \rangle$.
cards.body:
$\frac{22}{5}$

At $(1, 3)$: $\nabla f = \langle 2xy, x^2 \rangle = \langle 6, 1 \rangle$. Use the **unit vector** $\vec{u} = \langle 3, 4 \rangle / 5$, so $D_{\vec{u}} f = \nabla f \cdot \vec{u} = \frac{18 + 4}{5} = \frac{22}{5}$.

Watch out: dotting with $\vec{v}$ itself gives $22$, which is wrong because $|\vec{v}| = 5 \neq 1$.
cards.searchQuery: directional derivative gradient dot unit vector example

cards.title: At a given point, in which direction does $f$ increase fastest, and what is that fastest rate?
cards.body:
Along $
abla f$, at rate $|
abla f|$.

Since $D_{\vec{u}} f = 
abla f \cdot \vec{u} = |
abla f|\cos	heta$, the value is largest at $	heta = 0$. So $f$ decreases fastest along $-
abla f$.

Why: $D_{\vec{u}} f = 0$ for $\vec{u} \perp 
abla f$, which is why $
abla f$ is normal to level curves.
Watch out: the unit vector $\vec{u}$ must have length $1$, or the dot product overstates the rate.
cards.searchQuery: gradient direction of steepest ascent maximum rate of change

cards.title: At a critical point of $f(x, y)$, $D = f_{xx} f_{yy} - (f_{xy})^2 < 0$. What kind of point is it?
cards.body:
saddle point

The other cases: $D > 0$ and $f_{xx} > 0$ is a local **min**; $D > 0$ and $f_{xx} < 0$ is a local **max**; $D = 0$ is inconclusive.

Example: $f = x^2 - y^2$ at $(0, 0)$ has $D = (2)(-2) - 0^2 = -4$, a saddle.
Watch out: do not use the sign of $f_{xx}$ alone; $D$ decides first.
cards.searchQuery: second derivative test two variables saddle point discriminant

cards.title: To find extrema of $f(x, y)$ subject to $g(x, y) = k$, which equations do you solve?
cards.body:
$\nabla f = \lambda \nabla g$ together with $g(x, y) = k$ (where $\nabla g \neq \vec{0}$).

At a constrained extremum the level curve of $f$ is tangent to the constraint curve, so the **gradients are parallel**.

Tip: evaluate $f$ at every solution; if extremes exist, the largest value is the max and the smallest is the min.
Watch out: also check the constraint's endpoints or corners if the constraint region has boundary.
cards.searchQuery: Lagrange multipliers gradient f equals lambda gradient g constraint

cards.title: Converting a double integral to polar coordinates: $dA = \,?$
cards.body:
$r\,dr\,d\theta$

A small polar "rectangle" is about $r\,\Delta\theta$ wide and $\Delta r$ deep, so its area is $r\,\Delta r\,\Delta\theta$.

Example: the unit disk has area $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r\,dr\,d\theta = \pi$.
Watch out: dropping the factor $r$ gives $2\pi$, which is wrong.
cards.searchQuery: polar coordinates double integral area element r dr dtheta

cards.title: Spherical coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$: $dV = \underline{\quad}\ d\rho\,d\theta\,d\phi$
cards.body:
$\rho^2 \sin\phi$

Here $\phi$ is measured **down from the positive $z$-axis**, with $0 \le \phi \le \pi$.

Example: a ball of radius $R$ gives $\frac{R^3}{3}(2\pi)(2) = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3$.
Tip: cylindrical coordinates have $dV = r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$, with the same factor $r$ as polar.
cards.searchQuery: spherical coordinates volume element rho squared sin phi

cards.title: Change of variables $x = g(u, v)$, $y = h(u, v)$ in a double integral: $dA = \,?$
cards.body:
$dA = \left|\frac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(u, v)}\right| du\,dv$, where $\frac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(u, v)} = x_u y_v - x_v y_u$.

Example: $x = 2u + v$, $y = u - 3v$ gives $(2)(-3) - (1)(1) = -7$, so $dA = 7\,du\,dv$.

Watch out: take the **absolute value** of the Jacobian.
Tip: for polar coordinates the Jacobian is $r$.
cards.searchQuery: Jacobian change of variables double integral formula

cards.title: How do you test whether $\vec{F} = \langle P, Q \rangle$ is conservative, and what does that give you?
cards.body:
Check $\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}$ on an open, simply connected region (in 3D, check $\nabla \times \vec{F} = \vec{0}$).

Then $\vec{F} = \nabla f$, so $\int_C \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = f(\text{end}) - f(\text{start})$. The integral is **path-independent**, and $0$ around closed curves.

Example: $\langle 2xy, x^2 \rangle = \nabla(x^2 y)$.
Watch out: the region must have no holes; $\langle -y, x \rangle / (x^2 + y^2)$ passes the test but is not conservative on the punctured plane.
cards.searchQuery: conservative vector field test partial derivatives path independence

cards.title: Green's Theorem: $\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D (\,?\,)\,dA$ for positively oriented $C$. What goes in the blank?
cards.body:
$\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}$

$C$ is a counterclockwise, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve bounding $D$.

Example: area shortcut $A = \oint_C x\,dy = \frac{1}{2}\oint_C (x\,dy - y\,dx)$.
Watch out: $P_y - Q_x$ flips the sign.
cards.searchQuery: Green's theorem circulation form Q_x minus P_y

cards.title: For $\vec{F} = \langle P, Q, R \rangle$, what are $\operatorname{div}\vec{F}$ and $\operatorname{curl}\vec{F}$?
cards.body:
$\operatorname{div}\vec{F} = P_x + Q_y + R_z$ (a scalar); $\operatorname{curl}\vec{F} = \langle R_y - Q_z,\ P_z - R_x,\ Q_x - P_y angle$ (a vector).

These are $
abla \cdot \vec{F}$ and $
abla 	imes \vec{F}$.

Key idea: with continuous second partials, $
abla 	imes (
abla f) = \vec{0}$ and $
abla \cdot (
abla 	imes \vec{F}) = 0$.
cards.searchQuery: divergence and curl of a vector field formulas

cards.title: Stokes' Theorem: $\oint_C \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r}$ equals what surface integral, and how are $C$ and $S$ oriented?
cards.body:
$\iint_S (\nabla \times \vec{F}) \cdot d\vec{S}$, where $C$ is the boundary of the oriented surface $S$.

Use the **right-hand rule**: thumb along $S$'s normal, fingers curl in $C$'s direction. Equivalently, walking along $C$ with your head along the normal, $S$ stays on your left.

Key idea: Green's Theorem is the flat special case with $S$ in the $xy$-plane.
cards.searchQuery: Stokes theorem line integral surface integral curl orientation

cards.title: Find the outward flux of $\vec{F} = \langle x, y, z \rangle$ through the unit sphere.
cards.body:
$4\pi$

Divergence Theorem: $\iint_S \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{S} = \iiint_E \nabla \cdot \vec{F}\,dV$ for a closed surface $S$ oriented outward around the solid $E$.

Example: here $\nabla \cdot \vec{F} = 3$, so the flux is $3 \cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi = 4\pi$.
Watch out: the surface must be closed and oriented outward.
cards.searchQuery: divergence theorem flux unit sphere 4 pi

cards.title: What is a level curve of $f(x, y)$, and what do the level curves of $f = x^2 + y^2$ look like?
cards.body:
A level curve is the set where $f(x, y) = k$ for a constant $k$. For $f = x^2 + y^2$ they are **circles** centered at the origin with radius $\sqrt{k}$ ($k > 0$).

The level curves are the graph's slices at height $z = k$, projected onto the $xy$-plane. Closely spaced curves mean $f$ changes quickly there.

Key idea: $\nabla f$ is always perpendicular to the level curve through the point.
cards.searchQuery: level curves contour map function of two variables

cards.title: Describe the domain of $f(x, y) = \sqrt{4 - x^2 - y^2}$ as an inequality.
cards.body:
$x^2 + y^2 \le 4$

The square root needs $4 - x^2 - y^2 \ge 0$. That is the **closed disk** of radius $2$ centered at the origin.

Watch out: the graph is the upper hemisphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 4$, $z \ge 0$, and the range is $[0, 2]$.
cards.searchQuery: domain of function of two variables square root disk

cards.title: How do you show that $\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)} f(x, y)$ does not exist?
cards.body:
Find **two different paths** to $(0, 0)$ along which $f$ approaches different values.

Example: for $f = \frac{xy}{x^2 + y^2}$, along $y = 0$ the value is $0$, but along $y = x$ it is $\frac{x^2}{2x^2} = \frac{1}{2}$. So the limit does not exist.

Watch out: agreeing on every line you try proves nothing. To show a limit exists you need a squeeze or a polar-coordinate argument.
cards.searchQuery: limit does not exist two paths multivariable limit

cards.title: Evaluate $\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)} \frac{x^2 y}{x^2 + y^2}$.
cards.body:
$0$

Switch to polar: the expression is $\frac{r^3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta}{r^2} = r\cos^2\theta\sin\theta$. Its absolute value is at most $r$, which goes to $0$ as $(x, y) \to (0, 0)$.

Tip: use polar coordinates when the denominator is $x^2 + y^2$; the bound must not depend on $\theta$.
cards.searchQuery: two variable limit polar coordinates squeeze x^2 y over x^2 + y^2

cards.title: Write the limit definition of the partial derivative $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(a, b)$.
cards.body:
$f_x(a, b) = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{f(a + h, b) - f(a, b)}{h}$

Only $x$ moves; $y$ is held fixed at $b$. So $f_x$ is the **slope of the slice** of the graph in the plane $y = b$.

Tip: in practice, treat every other variable as a constant and use ordinary one-variable rules.
cards.searchQuery: partial derivative limit definition slope of slice

cards.title: Find $\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(x e^{xy}\right)$.
cards.body:
$x^2 e^{xy}$

Hold $x$ fixed. The chain rule on $e^{xy}$ gives $e^{xy}\cdot x$, and the leading factor $x$ stays: $x \cdot x e^{xy}$.

Watch out: the inner derivative of $xy$ with respect to $y$ is $x$, not $1$.
cards.searchQuery: partial derivative exponential x e^(xy) with respect to y

cards.title: Find $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\ln(x^2 + y^2)$.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{2x}{x^2 + y^2}$

By the chain rule, $\frac{1}{x^2 + y^2}$ times the derivative of the inside in $x$, which is $2x$ (the $y^2$ is a constant).

Example: by symmetry, $\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\ln(x^2 + y^2) = \frac{2y}{x^2 + y^2}$.
cards.searchQuery: partial derivative ln(x^2+y^2) with respect to x

cards.title: Find $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(x \sin(xy)\right)$.
cards.body:
$\sin(xy) + xy\cos(xy)$

Use the product rule on $x$ and $\sin(xy)$. The second factor's $x$-derivative is $\cos(xy)\cdot y$.

Watch out: both factors depend on $x$, so the product rule is required.
cards.searchQuery: partial derivative product rule x sin(xy)

cards.title: For $f(x, y) = x^3 y^2$, find $f_{yy}$.
cards.body:
$2x^3$

First $f_y = 2x^3 y$, then differentiate again in $y$.

Example: $f_{xx} = 6xy^2$ and $f_{xy} = f_{yx} = 6x^2 y$, so every mixed partial agrees, as Clairaut predicts.
cards.searchQuery: second order partial derivative f_yy x^3 y^2

cards.title: What is Laplace's equation for $u(x, y)$, and is $u = x^2 - y^2$ a solution?
cards.body:
$u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0$, and yes: $u = x^2 - y^2$ satisfies it.

Here $u_{xx} = 2$ and $u_{yy} = -2$, which sum to $0$. Solutions are called **harmonic functions**.

Watch out: $x^2 + y^2$ is not harmonic; its Laplacian is $2 + 2 = 4$.
cards.searchQuery: Laplace's equation harmonic function partial derivatives example

cards.title: Chain rule: $z = f(x, y)$ with $x = x(t)$ and $y = y(t)$. What is $\frac{dz}{dt}$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{dz}{dt} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\dfrac{dx}{dt} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\dfrac{dy}{dt}$

Each path from $z$ to $t$ in the tree diagram contributes one product, and you **add the paths**.

Watch out: use $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}$ for $f$ (several variables) but $\frac{d}{dt}$ for $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ (one variable).
cards.searchQuery: multivariable chain rule one parameter dz/dt formula

cards.title: $z = x^2 y$ with $x = t^2$ and $y = t^3$. Use the chain rule to find $\frac{dz}{dt}$ at $t = 1$.
cards.body:
$7$

At $t = 1$: $x = y = 1$, so $f_x = 2xy = 2$ and $f_y = x^2 = 1$; also $x'(1) = 2$ and $y'(1) = 3$. Then $\frac{dz}{dt} = 2\cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 3 = 7$.

Tip: check by substituting first: $z = t^7$, so $\frac{dz}{dt} = 7t^6 = 7$ at $t = 1$.
cards.searchQuery: chain rule example z = x^2 y x = t^2 y = t^3

cards.title: Chain rule: $z = f(x, y)$ with $x = x(s, t)$ and $y = y(s, t)$. What is $\frac{\partial z}{\partial s}$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial s} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial s}$

For $\frac{\partial z}{\partial t}$, replace $s$ with $t$ throughout.

Tip: draw a tree: $z$ branches to $x$ and $y$, and each branches to $s$ and $t$. Multiply along a branch, add across branches.
cards.searchQuery: chain rule two independent variables partial derivative tree diagram

cards.title: If $F(x, y) = 0$ defines $y$ implicitly as a function of $x$, what is $\frac{dy}{dx}$?
cards.body:
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{F_x}{F_y}$, provided $F_y \neq 0$.

If $F(x, y, z) = 0$ defines $z$ implicitly, then $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = -\frac{F_x}{F_z}$ and $\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = -\frac{F_y}{F_z}$.

Why: differentiate $F(x, y(x)) = 0$ with the chain rule: $F_x + F_y \frac{dy}{dx} = 0$.
cards.searchQuery: implicit differentiation partial derivatives -Fx/Fy formula

cards.title: Find the slope $\frac{dy}{dx}$ of $x^2 + y^2 = 25$ at $(3, 4)$.
cards.body:
$-\frac{3}{4}$

Take $F = x^2 + y^2 - 25$. Then $\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{F_x}{F_y} = -\frac{2x}{2y} = -\frac{x}{y}$, which is $-\frac{3}{4}$ at $(3, 4)$.

Tip: the tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius, whose slope is $\frac{4}{3}$; the negative reciprocal is $-\frac{3}{4}$.
cards.searchQuery: implicit differentiation slope of circle x^2+y^2=25 at (3,4)

cards.title: $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9$ defines $z$ implicitly. Find $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ at $(1, 2, 2)$.
cards.body:
$-\frac{1}{2}$

With $F = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 9$: $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = -\frac{F_x}{F_z} = -\frac{2x}{2z} = -\frac{x}{z} = -\frac{1}{2}$.

Watch out: $z$ depends on $x$ and $y$, so you cannot treat it as a constant when differentiating.
cards.searchQuery: implicit partial derivative dz/dx sphere x^2+y^2+z^2=9

cards.title: What is the linearization $L(x, y)$ of $f$ at $(a, b)$?
cards.body:
$L(x, y) = f(a, b) + f_x(a, b)(x - a) + f_y(a, b)(y - b)$

It is the tangent plane written as a function, and it approximates $f$ near $(a, b)$ when $f$ is differentiable there.

Key idea: in differential form, $\Delta f \approx f_x\,\Delta x + f_y\,\Delta y = df$.
cards.searchQuery: linearization two variables tangent plane approximation formula

cards.title: Use the linearization of $f(x, y) = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ at $(3, 4)$ to estimate $f(3.03, 3.96)$.
cards.body:
$4.986$

At $(3, 4)$: $f = 5$, $f_x = \frac{x}{f} = \frac{3}{5}$, $f_y = \frac{y}{f} = \frac{4}{5}$. So $L = 5 + 0.6(0.03) + 0.8(-0.04) = 5 + 0.018 - 0.032$.

Example: the exact value is about $4.9862$, so the estimate is close.
Watch out: $\Delta y = 3.96 - 4 = -0.04$ is negative.
cards.searchQuery: linear approximation estimate sqrt(x^2+y^2) near (3,4)

cards.title: What is the gradient $\nabla f$ of a function $f(x, y, z)$, and what does it point toward?
cards.body:
$\nabla f = \langle f_x, f_y, f_z \rangle$, a **vector of the partial derivatives**.

At each point it points in the direction of steepest increase of $f$, and it is perpendicular to the level surface through that point.

Example: $f = x^2 y + z$ gives $\nabla f = \langle 2xy, x^2, 1 \rangle$.
cards.searchQuery: gradient vector definition partial derivatives meaning

cards.title: Find $\nabla f(1, 2, 2)$ for $f(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2$.
cards.body:
$\langle 2, 4, 4 \rangle$

Since $\nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y, 2z \rangle$, plugging in $(1, 2, 2)$ gives $\langle 2, 4, 4 \rangle$.

Example: its length is $\sqrt{4 + 16 + 16} = 6$, which is the maximum directional derivative at that point.
cards.searchQuery: gradient of f at a point x^2+y^2+z^2 example

cards.title: Find the tangent plane to the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9$ at $(1, 2, 2)$.
cards.body:
$x + 2y + 2z = 9$

The gradient $\nabla F = \langle 2x, 2y, 2z \rangle = \langle 2, 4, 4 \rangle$ is normal to a level surface. Use $\langle 1, 2, 2 \rangle$ and the point-normal form: $(x - 1) + 2(y - 2) + 2(z - 2) = 0$.

Tip: general rule: tangent plane to $F = k$ at $P$ is $\nabla F(P) \cdot (\vec{r} - \vec{r}_P) = 0$.
cards.searchQuery: tangent plane to level surface using gradient sphere

cards.title: $f(x, y) = x^2 y$. What is the maximum rate of change of $f$ at $(1, 3)$?
cards.body:
$\sqrt{37}$

The maximum rate is $|\nabla f|$, attained in the direction of $\nabla f$. At $(1, 3)$, $\nabla f = \langle 6, 1 \rangle$, so $|\nabla f| = \sqrt{36 + 1} = \sqrt{37}$.

Watch out: the maximum rate is a length, so it is not $6 + 1$ and it is not the vector itself.
cards.searchQuery: maximum rate of change magnitude of gradient example

cards.title: Find the critical point of $f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 6y$.
cards.body:
$(2, -3)$

Set both partials to $0$: $f_x = 2x - 4 = 0$ gives $x = 2$, and $f_y = 2y + 6 = 0$ gives $y = -3$.

Key idea: a **critical point** is where $f_x = f_y = 0$ (or a partial does not exist). Here $f_{xx} = f_{yy} = 2 > 0$ and $f_{xy} = 0$, so $D = 4 > 0$: a local minimum.
cards.searchQuery: critical points of function of two variables find partial derivatives zero

cards.title: Classify the critical point $(0, 0)$ of $f(x, y) = x^2 + xy + y^2$.
cards.body:
local minimum

Here $f_{xx} = 2$, $f_{yy} = 2$ and $f_{xy} = 1$, so $D = (2)(2) - 1^2 = 3 > 0$. With $f_{xx} > 0$ the point is a local **minimum**.

Why: $x^2 + xy + y^2 = \left(x + \frac{y}{2}\right)^2 + \frac{3}{4}y^2 \ge 0$, with equality only at $(0, 0)$.
Watch out: do not read the cross term $xy$ as signalling a saddle; only the sign of $D$ decides.
cards.searchQuery: classify critical point second derivative test local minimum x^2+xy+y^2

cards.title: Find and classify the critical points of $f(x, y) = x^3 + y^3 - 3xy$.
cards.body:
$(0, 0)$ is a saddle point and $(1, 1)$ is a local minimum.

$f_x = 3x^2 - 3y = 0$ and $f_y = 3y^2 - 3x = 0$ give $y = x^2$ and $x = y^2$, so $x = x^4$ and $x = 0$ or $1$. Then $D = 36xy - 9$.

Example: $D(0, 0) = -9 < 0$ is a saddle; $D(1, 1) = 27 > 0$ with $f_{xx} = 6 > 0$ is a min.
cards.searchQuery: classify critical points x^3 + y^3 - 3xy saddle local minimum

cards.title: State the Extreme Value Theorem for a function of two variables.
cards.body:
If $f$ is **continuous** on a **closed and bounded** set $D \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, then $f$ attains an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on $D$.

Both hypotheses matter. On the open disk $x^2 + y^2 < 1$, $f = x$ has no maximum; on the unbounded plane, $f = x$ has neither.

Tip: when the theorem applies, you are guaranteed that checking critical points and the boundary finds the answer.
cards.searchQuery: extreme value theorem two variables closed bounded set continuous

cards.title: What are the steps to find the absolute extrema of $f(x, y)$ on a closed, bounded region $D$?
cards.body:
1. Find the critical points of $f$ in the interior of $D$ and compute $f$ there.
2. Find the extreme values of $f$ **on the boundary** (parametrize it, or use Lagrange multipliers).
3. Compare all values; the largest is the absolute max and the smallest is the absolute min.

Watch out: do not skip the boundary, and include corner points of the boundary as candidates.
cards.searchQuery: absolute maximum minimum closed region steps interior boundary

cards.title: Find the maximum of $f(x, y) = x + 2y$ on the disk $x^2 + y^2 \le 5$.
cards.body:
$5$

There are no interior critical points ($\nabla f = \langle 1, 2 \rangle \neq \vec{0}$), so the max is on the circle. Lagrange: $\langle 1, 2 \rangle = \lambda\langle 2x, 2y \rangle$ gives $y = 2x$, so $5x^2 = 5$ and $(x, y) = (1, 2)$.

Tip: check with Cauchy-Schwarz: $x + 2y \le |\langle 1, 2 \rangle|\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \sqrt{5}\sqrt{5} = 5$.
cards.searchQuery: maximum of linear function on a disk Lagrange multipliers x+2y

cards.title: Maximize $xy$ subject to $x + y = 10$. What is the maximum value?
cards.body:
$25$

Solve $\langle y, x \rangle = \lambda\langle 1, 1 \rangle$, so $x = y$. With $x + y = 10$, both equal $5$, and $xy = 25$.

Tip: a one-variable check: $x(10 - x)$ is a downward parabola with vertex at $x = 5$.
cards.searchQuery: Lagrange multipliers maximize xy subject to x+y=10

cards.title: What does the multiplier $\lambda$ measure in the method of Lagrange multipliers?
cards.body:
$\lambda$ is the **rate of change of the optimal value** of $f$ as the constraint level $k$ in $g = k$ changes.

In economics it is the shadow price: how much the best achievable value improves per unit of extra budget.

Example: for $xy$ with $x + y = k$, the max is $\frac{k^2}{4}$ and $\lambda = \frac{k}{2}$, which equals $\frac{d}{dk}\frac{k^2}{4}$.
cards.searchQuery: meaning of Lagrange multiplier lambda shadow price rate of change

cards.title: With two constraints $g = k$ and $h = l$, what equations does the Lagrange method use for extrema of $f(x, y, z)$?
cards.body:
$
abla f = \lambda
abla g + \mu
abla h$, together with $g = k$ and $h = l$.

The two constraints cut out a curve; at an extremum $
abla f$ must be perpendicular to that curve, so it lies in the plane spanned by $
abla g$ and $
abla h$.

Watch out: you now have five equations in five unknowns $x, y, z, \lambda, \mu$.
cards.searchQuery: Lagrange multipliers two constraints gradient lambda mu

cards.title: Use Lagrange multipliers to find the shortest distance from the origin to the plane $x + 2y + 3z = 14$.
cards.body:
$\sqrt{14}$

Minimize $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ with $\langle 2x, 2y, 2z \rangle = \lambda\langle 1, 2, 3 \rangle$, so $(x, y, z) = t(1, 2, 3)$. The constraint gives $14t = 14$, so $t = 1$ and the point is $(1, 2, 3)$ at distance $\sqrt{14}$.

Tip: minimizing the squared distance avoids the square root and has the same minimizer.
cards.searchQuery: shortest distance from origin to plane Lagrange multipliers

cards.title: What does $\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$ mean for $f \ge 0$, and how is it defined?
cards.body:
It is the **volume** of the solid under the graph $z = f(x, y)$ and above the region $R$.

It is the limit of Riemann sums $\sum f(x_i^*, y_j^*)\,\Delta A$ as the cells shrink. With $f = 1$ it gives the area of $R$.

Key idea: for continuous $f$ on a rectangle, **Fubini's Theorem** lets you compute it as an iterated integral in either order.
cards.searchQuery: double integral definition volume under surface Riemann sum

cards.title: Evaluate $\int_0^1\int_0^2 xy^2\,dy\,dx$.
cards.body:
$\frac{4}{3}$

Inner integral in $y$: $x\cdot\frac{y^3}{3}\Big|_0^2 = \frac{8x}{3}$. Outer: $\int_0^1 \frac{8x}{3}\,dx = \frac{8}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{2} = \frac{4}{3}$.

Tip: the integrand factors as $x \cdot y^2$ over a rectangle, so the result is $\left(\int_0^1 x\,dx\right)\left(\int_0^2 y^2\,dy\right) = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{8}{3}$.
cards.searchQuery: evaluate iterated double integral rectangle xy^2

cards.title: Evaluate $\int_0^1\int_x^1 e^{y^2}\,dy\,dx$ by reversing the order.
cards.body:
$\frac{e - 1}{2}$

The region is $0 \le x \le y \le 1$. Reversed, it is $0 \le y \le 1$ and $0 \le x \le y$, so the integral is $\int_0^1 y\,e^{y^2}\,dy = \frac{1}{2}\left(e - 1\right)$.

Tip: when an inner integral has no elementary antiderivative, **sketch the region and swap the order**.
cards.searchQuery: reverse order of integration e^(y^2) double integral

cards.title: Use a double integral to find the area of the region between $y = x^2$ and $y = x$.
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{6}$

The curves meet at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, with $x^2 \le y \le x$ in between. So $A = \int_0^1\int_{x^2}^{x} dy\,dx = \int_0^1 (x - x^2)\,dx = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}$.

Tip: identify the top and bottom curves before setting limits; the inner limits may depend on the outer variable.
cards.searchQuery: area between parabola and line double integral type I region

cards.title: What is the average value of $f(x, y) = xy$ over the rectangle $[0, 2] \times [0, 3]$?
cards.body:
$\frac{3}{2}$

The average value is $\frac{1}{A(R)}\iint_R f\,dA$. Here $\iint_R xy\,dA = \left(\int_0^2 x\,dx\right)\left(\int_0^3 y\,dy\right) = 2\cdot\frac{9}{2} = 9$, and the area is $6$.

Watch out: dividing by the area is essential; $9$ is the total, not the average.
cards.searchQuery: average value of function over rectangle double integral

cards.title: Find the volume under $z = 4 - x - y$ over the square $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$.
cards.body:
$3$

$\int_0^1\int_0^1 (4 - x - y)\,dy\,dx = 4 - \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} = 3$.

Tip: since the region has area $1$, the volume equals the average height, which is the height at the center $(0.5, 0.5)$: $4 - 1 = 3$ (true for a plane).
cards.searchQuery: volume under plane over square double integral

cards.title: Evaluate $\iint_D (x^2 + y^2)\,dA$ over the unit disk $D$.
cards.body:
$\frac{\pi}{2}$

In polar form $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ and $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$, so the integral is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r^3\,dr\,d\theta = 2\pi\cdot\frac{1}{4}$.

Watch out: the integrand $r^2$ and the area factor $r$ multiply to give $r^3$.
cards.searchQuery: polar coordinates double integral over unit disk x^2+y^2

cards.title: Evaluate $\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} e^{-(x^2 + y^2)}\,dA$.
cards.body:
$\pi$

In polar: $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}\,r\,dr\,d\theta = 2\pi\cdot\frac{1}{2} = \pi$.

Key idea: the integral also equals $\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2}dx\right)^2$, which proves $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2}dx = \sqrt{\pi}$.
cards.searchQuery: Gaussian integral polar coordinates e^(-(x^2+y^2)) pi

cards.title: Find the area enclosed by the polar curve $r = 2\cos\theta$.
cards.body:
$\pi$

It is the circle of radius $1$ centered at $(1, 0)$, traced once for $-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$. Area: $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{1}{2}(2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} 2\cos^2\theta\,d\theta = \pi$.

Watch out: using $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$ traces the circle twice and doubles the answer.
cards.searchQuery: area enclosed by polar curve r = 2cos theta circle

cards.title: For a lamina occupying $D$ with density $\rho(x, y)$, what are the mass and the center of mass $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$?
cards.body:
$m = \iint_D \rho\,dA$, $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{m}\iint_D x\rho\,dA$ and $\bar{y} = \frac{1}{m}\iint_D y\rho\,dA$.

The integrals $\iint x\rho\,dA$ and $\iint y\rho\,dA$ are the moments about the $y$- and $x$-axes.

Tip: use symmetry first; if the region and density are symmetric about an axis, the center of mass lies on it.
cards.searchQuery: center of mass of lamina double integral density formula

cards.title: What is the area of the surface $z = f(x, y)$ over a region $D$?
cards.body:
$A = \iint_D \sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2}\,dA$

The factor $\sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2} = |\langle -f_x, -f_y, 1 \rangle|$ is the stretch from flat area $dA$ to tilted surface area.

Example: for a plane $z = x + 2y$ the factor is $\sqrt{6}$, so the surface area is $\sqrt{6}\cdot\text{Area}(D)$.
cards.searchQuery: surface area of graph z=f(x,y) double integral formula

cards.title: Evaluate $\iiint_B xyz\,dV$ over the box $B = [0, 1] \times [0, 2] \times [0, 3]$.
cards.body:
$\frac{9}{2}$

The integrand is a product of one-variable functions over a box, so the integral factors: $\int_0^1 x\,dx \cdot \int_0^2 y\,dy \cdot \int_0^3 z\,dz = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot\frac{9}{2}$.

Watch out: factoring works only when the region is a box (constant limits).
cards.searchQuery: triple integral over rectangular box xyz example

cards.title: What are the conversion formulas for cylindrical coordinates $(r, \theta, z)$, and what is $dV$?
cards.body:
$x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, $z = z$, with $r^2 = x^2 + y^2$, and $dV = r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$.

Cylindrical coordinates are polar coordinates in the $xy$-plane plus the same height $z$.

Tip: use them for solids with an axis of symmetry along $z$, such as cylinders, cones and paraboloids.
cards.searchQuery: cylindrical coordinates conversion formulas volume element

cards.title: What are the conversion formulas from spherical coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ to $(x, y, z)$?
cards.body:
$x = \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta$, $y = \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta$, $z = \rho\cos\phi$, and $\rho^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2$.

Here $\rho \ge 0$ is the distance from the origin, $\phi \in [0, \pi]$ is the angle down from the $+z$-axis, and $\theta$ is the same azimuth as in polar coordinates.

Watch out: textbooks in physics swap the roles of $\theta$ and $\phi$; here $\phi$ is the polar angle from the $z$-axis.
cards.searchQuery: spherical coordinates to rectangular conversion formulas rho phi theta

cards.title: Convert the spherical point $(\rho, \theta, \phi) = \left(2, \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ to rectangular coordinates.
cards.body:
$(0, 2, 0)$

$x = 2\sin\frac{\pi}{2}\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0$, $y = 2\sin\frac{\pi}{2}\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 2$, and $z = 2\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0$.

Tip: $\phi = \frac{\pi}{2}$ puts the point in the $xy$-plane, and $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$ points along the positive $y$-axis.
cards.searchQuery: convert spherical coordinates to rectangular example

cards.title: Use cylindrical coordinates to find the volume of the solid between $z = r$ and $z = 1$.
cards.body:
$\frac{\pi}{3}$

For each $r \in [0, 1]$, $z$ runs from $r$ to $1$. So $V = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1\int_r^1 r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta = 2\pi\int_0^1 (r - r^2)\,dr = 2\pi\left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}\right)$.

Example: this matches the cone formula $\frac{1}{3}\pi R^2 h = \frac{1}{3}\pi(1)^2(1)$.
cards.searchQuery: volume of cone cylindrical coordinates triple integral z = r

cards.title: Evaluate $\iiint_B \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\,dV$ over the unit ball $B$.
cards.body:
$\pi$

In spherical coordinates the integrand is $\rho$, so $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^1 \rho\cdot\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta = 2\pi\cdot 2\cdot\frac{1}{4}$.

Tip: whenever $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ appears, switch to spherical; $\rho^2$ replaces it.
cards.searchQuery: triple integral unit ball spherical coordinates distance from origin

cards.title: Use $x = au$, $y = bv$ to find the area enclosed by the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$.
cards.body:
$\pi ab$

The Jacobian is $\frac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(u, v)} = ab$, and the ellipse maps to the unit disk $u^2 + v^2 \le 1$. So the area is $ab\cdot\pi(1)^2$.

Tip: a linear stretch multiplies areas by the constant $ab$.
cards.searchQuery: area of ellipse Jacobian change of variables pi ab

cards.title: With $u = x + y$ and $v = x - y$, $dx\,dy = \underline{\quad}\ du\,dv$. What constant fills the blank?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{2}$

The Jacobian of $(u, v)$ with respect to $(x, y)$ is $(1)(-1) - (1)(1) = -2$, and $\frac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(u, v)}$ is its reciprocal, $-\frac{1}{2}$. Take the absolute value.

Watch out: using $2$ instead of $\frac{1}{2}$ is the classic slip; the two Jacobians are **reciprocals**.
cards.searchQuery: Jacobian reciprocal u = x+y v = x-y change of variables

cards.title: What is a vector field, and what is a simple example?
cards.body:
A vector field assigns a **vector** to each point of a region: $\vec{F}(x, y) = \langle P(x, y), Q(x, y) \rangle$ in the plane.

Example: $\vec{F} = \langle -y, x \rangle$ gives a counterclockwise rotation about the origin; the gradient $\nabla f$ of any scalar function is a vector field too.

Tip: sketch a field by drawing the vector at several points; its length is the field's strength there.
cards.searchQuery: vector field definition examples plane rotation field

cards.title: How do you compute the scalar line integral $\int_C f\,ds$ for a curve $\vec{r}(t)$, $a \le t \le b$?
cards.body:
$\int_C f\,ds = \int_a^b f(\vec{r}(t))\,|\vec{r}\,'(t)|\,dt$

The factor $|\vec{r}\,'(t)|\,dt$ is the arc length element $ds$. With $f = 1$ the integral gives the length of $C$.

Key idea: it does **not** depend on the direction in which $C$ is traversed.
cards.searchQuery: scalar line integral arc length element formula parametrized curve

cards.title: Evaluate $\int_C (x^2 + y^2)\,ds$ where $C$ is the circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin.
cards.body:
$16\pi$

On $C$ the integrand is constantly $x^2 + y^2 = 4$. So the integral is $4\cdot(\text{length of } C) = 4\cdot 4\pi$.

Tip: when $f$ is constant on the curve, just multiply by the arc length.
cards.searchQuery: scalar line integral over circle constant integrand arc length

cards.title: How do you compute the work integral $\int_C \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$ for $\vec{r}(t)$, $a \le t \le b$?
cards.body:
$\int_C \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = \int_a^b \vec{F}(\vec{r}(t))\cdot\vec{r}\,'(t)\,dt$

It adds up the component of $\vec{F}$ along the direction of motion.

Watch out: unlike the scalar line integral, reversing the direction of $C$ **flips the sign**.
cards.searchQuery: line integral of vector field work formula F dot r prime

cards.title: Find the work done by $\vec{F} = \langle -y, x \rangle$ around the circle of radius $2$, counterclockwise.
cards.body:
$8\pi$

Parametrize $\vec{r}(t) = \langle 2\cos t, 2\sin t \rangle$, so $\vec{r}\,'(t) = \langle -2\sin t, 2\cos t \rangle$. Then $\vec{F}\cdot\vec{r}\,' = 4\sin^2 t + 4\cos^2 t = 4$ and $\int_0^{2\pi} 4\,dt = 8\pi$.

Example: Green's Theorem agrees: $Q_x - P_y = 2$, times the area $4\pi$.
cards.searchQuery: work done vector field around circle line integral -y x

cards.title: State the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals.
cards.body:
If $\vec{F} = \nabla f$ with $f$ continuously differentiable, then $\int_C \nabla f\cdot d\vec{r} = f(\vec{r}(b)) - f(\vec{r}(a))$.

Only the endpoints matter, so the integral is **path independent**; around a closed curve it is $0$.

Watch out: this requires a potential function $f$; if $\vec{F}$ is not conservative the theorem does not apply.
cards.searchQuery: fundamental theorem for line integrals gradient endpoints path independent

cards.title: Evaluate $\int_C \langle 2xy,\ x^2,\ 1 \rangle\cdot d\vec{r}$ along any path from $(0, 0, 0)$ to $(1, 2, 3)$.
cards.body:
$5$

The field is $\nabla f$ for the potential $f = x^2 y + z$. Then the integral is $f(1, 2, 3) - f(0, 0, 0) = 2 + 3 - 0 = 5$.

Tip: check $\nabla f$: $\langle 2xy, x^2, 1 \rangle$ matches the field exactly.
cards.searchQuery: line integral conservative field potential function endpoints example

cards.title: Find a potential function $f$ with $\nabla f = \langle 2xy + 3,\ x^2 + 2y \rangle$ (leave out $+C$).
cards.body:
$f = x^2 y + 3x + y^2$

Integrate $f_x = 2xy + 3$ in $x$: $f = x^2 y + 3x + g(y)$. Then $f_y = x^2 + g'(y)$ must equal $x^2 + 2y$, so $g(y) = y^2$.

Tip: check by differentiating: $f_x = 2xy + 3$ and $f_y = x^2 + 2y$.
cards.searchQuery: find potential function of conservative vector field integrate partial

cards.title: Use Green's Theorem to evaluate $\oint_C -y^3\,dx + x^3\,dy$, with $C$ the unit circle traversed counterclockwise.
cards.body:
$\frac{3\pi}{2}$

Here $Q_x - P_y = 3x^2 - (-3y^2) = 3(x^2 + y^2)$. In polar coordinates, $\iint_D 3r^2\,dA = 3\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r^3\,dr\,d\theta = 3\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}$.

Watch out: with $P = -y^3$, $P_y = -3y^2$, so subtracting it adds $3y^2$.

cards.title: For the graph $z = g(x, y)$ with upward normal, how do you compute $\iint_S \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{S}$ for $\vec{F} = \langle P, Q, R \rangle$?
cards.body:
$\iint_D \left(-P\,g_x - Q\,g_y + R\right)dA$, evaluated at $z = g(x, y)$ over the projection $D$.

The upward normal vector is $\langle -g_x, -g_y, 1 \rangle$, and $d\vec{S} = \langle -g_x, -g_y, 1 \rangle\,dA$.

Watch out: for a downward orientation, flip the sign of the whole integral.

cards.title: Compute $\nabla \times \vec{F}$ for $\vec{F} = \langle z, x, y \rangle$.
cards.body:
$\langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle$

With $P = z$, $Q = x$, $R = y$: $R_y - Q_z = 1 - 0$, $P_z - R_x = 1 - 0$, $Q_x - P_y = 1 - 0$.

Tip: the curl is constant here, so this field is not conservative, since $\nabla \times \vec{F} \neq \vec{0}$.
cards.searchQuery: compute curl of vector field z x y

cards.title: Compute $\nabla \cdot \vec{F}$ for $\vec{F} = \langle x^2, y^2, z^2 \rangle$.
cards.body:
$2x + 2y + 2z$

Add the matching partials: $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}x^2 + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}y^2 + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}z^2$.

Watch out: the divergence is a scalar function, so the answer is not a vector.
cards.searchQuery: compute divergence of vector field x^2 y^2 z^2

cards.title: What do divergence and curl of a vector field measure physically?
cards.body:
**Divergence** measures net outflow per unit volume at a point: positive for a source, negative for a sink, $0$ for an incompressible flow.

**Curl** measures local rotation: it points along the axis of a tiny paddle wheel's spin, with magnitude equal to twice the angular speed.

Key idea: the Divergence Theorem and Stokes' Theorem turn these local measures into global flux and circulation.

cards.title: Find the length of the helix $\vec{r}(t) = \langle \cos t, \sin t, t \rangle$ for $0 \le t \le 2\pi$.
cards.body:
$2\pi\sqrt{2}$

Here $\vec{r}\,'(t) = \langle -\sin t, \cos t, 1 \rangle$ has constant length $\sqrt{2}$. So $L = \int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{2}\,dt$.

Key idea: arc length is $L = \int_a^b |\vec{r}\,'(t)|\,dt$, the integral of speed.
